The most common way is to use an **interpolate** (smooth ramp) or a **step** (discrete buckets) expression.

Below are two complete examples – one with a smooth gradient and one with stepped colours – that you can drop into the `paint` section of your circle layer.

---

## 1. Smooth gradient (darker = higher population)

```json
{
  "id": "cities-circle",
  "type": "circle",
  "source": "my-data",          // whatever source you already have
  "source-layer": "cities",     // only needed for vector sources
  "paint": {
    "circle-radius": 6,
    "circle-color": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"],               // linear interpolation between stops
      ["get", "population"],    // the property to base the colour on
      0,    "#f2f0f7",          // lightest colour for 0 people
      1000, "#cbc9e2",
      5000, "#9e9ac8",
      20000, "#756bb1",
      50000, "#54278f"          // darkest colour for the biggest values
    ],
    "circle-opacity": 0.8
  }
}
```

**How it works**

| Part | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `"interpolate"` | Creates a continuous colour ramp. |
| `["linear"]` | Uses linear interpolation (you could also use `"exponential"` with a base). |
| `["get", "population"]` | Reads the `population` property from each feature. |
| The series of *stop* pairs (`value`, `color`) | Define the colour you want at specific population thresholds. MapLibre will smoothly blend between them. |

Adjust the stop values and colours to match the range of your data and the visual style you prefer.

---

## 2. Stepped colours (discrete buckets)

If you prefer distinct colour bands rather than a smooth gradient:

```json

  "type": "circle",
  "source": "my-data",
  "source-layer": "cities",

    "circle-color": [

      ["get", "population"],   // property to evaluate
      "#f2f0f7",               // default colour (population < 1 000)
      1000, "#cbc9e2",         // 1 000 ≤ pop < 5 000
      5000, "#9e9ac8",         // 5 000 ≤ pop < 20 000

    "circle-opacity": 0.8
  }
```

`step` works like a series of “if ≥ value then colour” checks, giving you crisp colour changes at the thresholds you define.
